newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico's Ortiz sets sights on 6 pct growth or more.
newsitem.headline: Mexico's Ortiz sets sights on 6 pct growth or more.

text.p: Mexican Finance Minister Guillermo Ortiz, facing questions from legislators about the country's lackluster economic performance, said on Tuesday the country needed growth rates of at least six percent and denied he was wedded to balanced budgets.

"I think a growth rate of four percent is insufficient for this country," Ortiz said in a question-and-answer session in Congress, referring to a level of growth in gross domestic product that the government would target in 1997.
"We should have much higher growth rates, of six or of seven percent," he said.

In his second State of the Nation address on Sunday, President Ernesto Zedillo declared that the country's 1994-95 economic crisis was over. He said next year's budget would reflect a growth assumption of at least four percent, rising still higher in 1998 and afterwards.
Still, legislators from all parties said many Mexicans had yet to benefit from the improving economy, and Ortiz was repeatedly pressed to introduce measures to boost jobs and salaries.

The minister said in 1997 the country could comfortably run a current account deficit, equivalent to two percent of GDP, arguing that Mexico was gaining the ability to shelter itself from external shocks.
He also denied that he was wedded to a balanced budget next year, and said a surplus in public finances in the first half of 1996 would free up more resources for social spending in the second half.
"I want to assure you...that there is no dogma in maintaining a strict balance in public finances," Ortiz said.
"Certainly to the degree that we can continue funding public finances in a healthy manner...it's possible that...there will be a deficit, but a moderate one (in 1997)," he said.
He noted that pressures on the budget will grow next year because of social security contributions and health reform.
